newsitem.title: ITALY: Itay's Ciampi defends budget as "step one" of plan.
newsitem.headline: Itay's Ciampi defends budget as "step one" of plan.

text.p: Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said on Monday the government's mini-budget approved by cabinet last week was only one of two steps in cleaning up state accounts and should not be judged on its own.

The centre-left coalition has come under heavy fire from opposition and industry for its 15.5 trillion lire ($9.2 billion) package of deficit cutting measures aimed at raising Italy's chances of joining Europe's currency union in 1999.
One of the latest critics was Nobel Prize-winning economist Franco Modigliani who wrote in a letter to Ciampi the additional budgetary measures were damaging and should be withdrawn.

"Withdraw the decree whose measures for the most part violate the elementary rules of accounting, harm the economy and above all the credibility of the government and the country," Modigliani wrote in the letter published in the daily Corriere della Sera newspaper at the weekend.
Ciampi replied in a letter published by Italian news agency ANSA that both quantitative and qualitative measures were needed to reorder Italy's state accounts.
"With the measures decided last Thursday the government provided for the quantitative side.

"Last Thursday the prime minister solemnly and publically undertook to deal with the qualitative aspects as well, to open up the necessary debate as soon as possible with the parties concerned," Ciampi wrote in his reply.
"The two instances make a whole and as such they should be considered jointly as the government's economic policy and its reason for being," he said.

Last week's mini-budget is designed to cut Italy's budget deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by the end of 1997 in time to meet tough economic criteria required to join Europe's economic and monetary union at its 1999 start. Italy had a deficit to GDP ratio of 6.7 percent in 1996.

Ciampi said quantitative measures were needed to cut the budget deficit but qualitative ones were also necessary "to give the certainty of stability, in particular pursuing equilibrium in the pension system in the framework of reconsidering the social state, a problem common to all industrial countries."

Modigliani, economist at the Massachussetts Institute of Technology (MIT), urged the government to replace the mini-budget after local council elections on April 27 with measures "perhaps more limited but serious and structural... as soon as possible but after mature consideration."

He said he was convinced "credibility is the most important ingredient to ensure Italy can enter Maastricht, out of principle, with dignity, with or without Germany. Otherwise wouldn't it be better to resign?"
